nodes.label: Education and AI
nodes.question: What are the three significant ways this research advances sociocultural learning theory?
nodes.answer: The research advances sociocultural learning theory by (1) explicating how AI competencies develop through social practice in underserved communities, (2) providing a comprehensive framework for equitable AI education integration, and (3) demonstrating how open schooling methodologies foster transformative learning experiences.
nodes.paragraph: KNOW (Applying Al) demonstrates how problem-solving, STEM for sustainability, and future prospects become embodied through application. DO (Creating Al) reveals how scientific citizenship and authentic learning with AI catalyse new forms of participa- tion. This research advances sociocultural learning theory in three significant ways: (1) it empirically explicates how Al competencies develop through social practice in underserved communities, challenging existing theoretical paradigms; (2) it provides a comprehensive, evidence-based framework for equitable Al education integra- tion across disciplines; and (3) it demonstrates how open schooling methodologies can foster transformative learning experiences that prepare students for an Al-driven future while promoting social justice and sustainable development. The findings have profound implications for educational policy and practice, suggesting a fundamental Extended author information available on the last page of the article International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education reconceptualization of Al literacy development in secondary education. This work establishes a new theoretical foundation for understanding how schools can system- atically develop Al competencies while addressing critical issues of equity, inclusion, and sustainable development in an increasingly Al-mediated world.

nodes.label: Theory
nodes.question: What theoretical framework does the study build upon to examine students' development of AI competencies?
nodes.answer: The study builds on Vygotsky's sociocultural theory, which emphasizes learning through social interaction and cultural tools.
nodes.paragraph: This study specifically looks at drivers and challenges faced by underserved stu- dents with emerging technologies such as Al, positioning them as not only consumers but also innovators and problem solvers for a sustainable future (Vinuesa et al., 2020). International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education Building on Vygotsky S (1978) sociocultural theory, which emphasises learning through social interaction and cultural tools, we examine how students develop AI competencies through collaborative knowledge construction and guided participation. The ability to adapt and co-create in the face of AI advancements is critical for both educators and life- long learners (Santana & D az-Fern ndez, 2023a, 2023b). Moreover, critical and crea- tive thinking is essential for fostering innovation and developing inclusive, diverse, and equitable solutions for society. As AI becomes an integral part of daily life (Miao, 2022), scientific, digital, and informational multiliteracies along with an understanding of eth- ics and sustainability are key. Transversal skills are essential for collaborative, interdis- ciplinary learning, enabling individuals to thrive in a world shaped by rapid technologi- cal evolution (Sofia et al., 2023; Kaplan & Haenlein, 2019).

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What does communicative learning focus on?
nodes.answer: Communicative learning focuses on interpersonal interactions and involves comprehending the meaning behind someone's communication.
nodes.paragraph: Mezirow categorizes learning into communicative and instrumental domains (Mezirow, 1991 , 2003 ). Communicative learning focuses on interpersonal interactions and involves comprehending the meaning behind someone S communication. The components of comprehension and interpretation include values, intentions, emotions, moral choices, and normative ideas (Mezirow, 1991 , 2003 ). Communicative learning enables people to navigate and interpret their meanings, intentions, and values rather than passively adopting those of others. Instrumental learning involves learning by doing (Mezirow, 1991 , 2003 ). It is a type of learning directed at a particular outcome and can help people become more effective at being and working in their environments (Zurba et al., 2021 ). Instrumental learning is especially relevant to the work of observers and can involve significant cognitive shifts that support transformation (Zurba et al., 2021 ). Contemporary scholars working with transformative learning theory have expanded their study to cultural, tacit, and emotional aspects of learning (Gozawa, 2009 ; Tisdell & Thompson, 2007 ; Cranton, 2006 ). For example, Cranton (2006 , p. 37) delineates transformative learning within the epistemic (knowledge-centered), sociolinguistic (society, norm, and culture-oriented), psychological (self-concept-focused), philosophical (worldview-centered), and aesthetic (broadly value-judgment oriented) ways of thinking (i.e., habits of mid), which are linked to content, process, and reflection.
